phonemes.desc: First syllable with voiced alveolar lateral approximant [l], final [ʊŋ] (close-mid back rounded vowel + velar nasal), and Tone 2 (rising, ˧˥). Pinyin 'o' before 'ng' corresponds to IPA [ʊ].
Second syllable with labial-velar glide [w], open vowel [a], velar nasal coda [ŋ], and Tone 2 (rising, ˧˥).

pronunciation.approximation: LUHNG-WAHNG — two even syllables, each rising from mid to high pitch; the 'o' of the first is like the 'oo' in 'book', the 'a' of the second like the 'a' in 'father'.

kin.label: Related terms
kin.form: 東海龍王 Dōnghǎi Lóngwáng (Dragon King of the East Sea); 敖廣 Āo Guǎng; 如意金箍棒 Rúyì Jīngū Bàng; 龍王廟 Lóngwáng miào (Dragon King temple)

pronunciation.note: 龍王 denotes the Dragon King, the crowned ruler of the waters in Chinese religion and literature. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is Lóngwáng — both syllables in Tone 2 (rising, ˧˥) — as recorded in the Unihan Database (Unicode Consortium, kMandarin) for 龍 and 王, and in standard Mandarin dictionaries. Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct the Old Chinese forms as *[m]-roŋ (龍, GSR 1193a) and *[ɢ]ʷaŋ (王). The tone-marked Pinyin restoration Lóngwáng preserves the citation rising tones of both syllables; in connected speech the contours may be compressed, but the lexical tones remain Tone 2 throughout.

domains.title: Kings of the Four Seas
domains.subtitle: Crystal Palaces, Rain by Mandate, the Bureaucracy of Water
domains.lead:
Lóngwáng, the Dragon King, is not one god but a crowned office — four brothers who hold the Four Seas that ring the Chinese world, each enthroned in an underwater crystal palace with its own court, treasury, and army of shrimp soldiers and crab generals. Āo Guǎng 敖廣 of the East Sea is the most prominent; beside him rule Āo Qīn 敖欽 of the South, Āo Rùn 敖閏 of the West, and Āo Shùn 敖順 of the North. Beneath them, lesser dragon kings govern every river, lake, and well worth the naming.

In their world, rainfall is a bureaucratic act. The Jade Emperor issues the mandate — how much rain, where, and at what hour — and the Dragon King delivers it, down to the last tenth of an inch. It is the Chinese imagination at its most characteristic: the wild water of heaven brought under a seal, a ledger, and a chain of command. The novels and the village temples agree on the stakes — a king who edits the figures loses his head, and a village that loses the king's favour loses its harvest.

cards.name: The Four Seas
cards.desc: Four royal brothers divide the encircling oceans — East, South, West, and North — each ruling tides, storms, and every creature of his sea from a crystal palace below the waves.

cards.name: Rain by Mandate
cards.desc: Rainfall is paperwork: the Jade Emperor decrees the amount and the hour, and the Dragon King executes the order exactly — to alter either is treason against heaven.

cards.name: The Sea Treasury
cards.desc: The crystal palace hoards the wealth of the waters — pearls, coral, and the Rúyì Jīngū Bàng, the iron pillar that once pinned the seas, until the Monkey King claimed it for a staff.

cards.name: Kingship under Heaven
cards.desc: The Dragon King is sovereign in his own water and a subject above it — a king who kneels to the celestial bureaucracy and answers with his life for every misplaced drop.

symbols.name: Crystal palace
symbols.meaning: The underwater court (龍宮, Dragon Palace) — sovereignty, hidden wealth, and the ordered world beneath the chaos of the sea

symbols.name: Rúyì Jīngū Bàng
symbols.meaning: The compliant gold-banded staff, an iron pillar that once pinned the seas — the tameable measure of the waters, taken from the East Sea treasury by Sūn Wùkōng

symbols.name: Dragon robe and royal crown
symbols.meaning: Enfeoffed kingship within the celestial bureaucracy — the Dragon King rules as a peer of heaven's administration, not as a free lord

symbols.name: Rain clouds and tidal bore
symbols.meaning: The waters he commands — rain, rivers, lakes, and tides delivered by decree, withheld in drought, unleashed in flood

symbols.name: Shrimp soldiers and crab generals
symbols.meaning: The aquatic retinue of the Dragon Palace — the sea's own creatures enrolled as a court, a mirror of the imperial administration below the waves

mythology.lead: The Dragon Kings stand at the crossing of two Chinas: the literary China of the great Ming novels, where they are foils, creditors, and comic bureaucrats, and the living China of the village temple, where they were the address to which a drought-stricken county sent its prayers. The same figure is mocked in the novel and begged in the field.

myths.title: The Jìng River Dragon King's Wager
myths.text: The Journey to the West preserves the great cautionary tale of the celestial bureaucracy. The Dragon King of the Jìng River wagers with a mortal fortune-teller over the next day's rain; when the Jade Emperor's decree arrives matching the diviner's figures exactly, the king — unwilling to lose — secretly alters the amount and delays the timing. The difference is trifling, and it does not matter. For editing heaven's paperwork he is sentenced to death and executed, a reminder that in a cosmos run as an administration, the smallest forged figure is treason.

myths.title: Nézhā and the Third Prince
myths.text: In the Investiture of the Gods (Féngshén Yǎnyì), the boy Nézhā, bathing in the eastern stream, shakes the East Sea crystal palace to its foundations with his magic sash. Āo Guǎng sends his third son, Āo Bǐng, to subdue the child; Nézhā kills the prince and plucks out his sinews to make a belt. Faced with the Dragon King's wrath against his family and his town, Nézhā answers with the terrible arithmetic of filial duty — he cuts himself apart, returning his flesh to his mother and his bones to his father, so that the debt dies with him.

myths.title: The Sea-Pinning Iron
myths.text: Needing a weapon worthy of him, Sūn Wùkōng descends to the East Sea treasury and passes over every blade and spear Āo Guǎng can offer. What he takes instead is the Rúyì Jīngū Bàng — the Compliant Gold-Banded Staff, a black iron pillar that once pinned the seas and measured the flood-waters of the world. To the Dragon King it was a fixture of the deep; to the Monkey King it shrinks to a needle behind the ear and grows to a pillar that props up heaven. The East Sea never got it back.

myths.title: Parading the King in the Sun
myths.text: Dragon King temples (龍王廟) dotted farming China, and when the rains failed, the village went to the temple: processions, offerings, and rain-prayers addressed to the local king as to a magistrate who had neglected his district. In extreme drought the negotiation turned coercive — the king's effigy was carried out and paraded in the burning sun, so that he might feel on his own lacquered scales the heat his fields were dying of. Few religions have made their god's accountability so literal.

lore.syncretism: The Dragon Kings are among the clearest cases of Buddhism and native Chinese religion merging into a single figure. Native Chinese water-dragon and river-god cults are ancient, but the named kings with submarine palaces, retinues, and treasuries owe much to the Indian nāgarājas — serpent kings of the waters — carried into China with the translated sūtras; Chinese translators rendered nāga as lóng (dragon), and the eight nāga kings of Buddhist scripture became native sea-kings. The relative weight of the Indian import against the older Chinese cult remains a matter of scholarly debate. Taoism then absorbed the kings wholesale into its celestial administration as rain officials answerable to the Jade Emperor. From China the figure travelled with the culture: in Japan the dragon kings appear as ryūō, kin to the sea-god Ryūjin of the undersea palace; in Korea as Yongwang, propitiated by fishing and farming villages alike; in Vietnam as Long Vương, guardian of waters and of the nation's own dragon genealogy.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Dragon King never fully retired. His temples still stand along China's coasts and rivers, and rain-processions to the local king persisted in the countryside into the twentieth century. In literature and performance he is a permanent stock character: every adaptation of the Journey to the West — opera, film, television, animation — must eventually send someone down to the crystal palace, whether to borrow a weapon or to wreck the court. The feud with Nézhā alone has carried him through a century of Chinese animation, from the 1979 feature Nézhā Nào Hǎi (Nezha Conquers the Dragon King) to the 2019 blockbuster Ne Zha, where the dragon clan's grievance drives the plot. In the modern idiom the Dragon King's palace remains a byword for fabulous drowned wealth, and the figure himself endures wherever Chinese fantasy needs a throne beneath the sea.
lore.extendedMeditation:
The Dragon King teaches that water is governed, not merely unleashed. In the Chinese imagination even rain is paperwork: every shower has an issuing authority, an amount, an hour, and a signature. This is not a failure of wonder but a different kind of wonder — the conviction that the wildest force in the farmer's world can be brought under seal and ledger, and that the price of that order is absolute accountability. The Jìng River king lost his head for a trifle of water and an hour's delay, because in a cosmos run as an administration there is no such thing as a small alteration.

To name a domain Lóngwáng is therefore to claim the throne under the waves: the palace where treasure and law are kept together, where the sea's own creatures wear the robes of ministers, and where a king may be sovereign of all he surveys and still answer for every drop. It is the oldest Chinese lesson about power — that it is real only when it is answerable.

sources.name: Ao Guang, Dragon King of the East Sea

lore.archaeology: The material cult behind the Dragon Kings is far older than the kings themselves. Shang oracle bones (c. 1250–1045 BCE) record rain sacrifices addressed to river and water powers, and Han texts describe rain-making rites performed with clay dragons — Dong Zhongshu's Chunqiu Fanlu gives the liturgy, and Wang Chong's Lunheng argues against it. Han mirrors and tomb reliefs show the older cosmic dragon of clouds and ascent, not yet a crowned bureaucrat. The named Dragon Kings of the Four Seas crystallize in medieval China under Buddhist influence: nāga kings with submarine palaces appear in translated sūtras from the early centuries CE, the Tang court formally enfeoffed the dragon kings of the Four Seas with royal titles, and by the Song their temples stood in the official register of sacrifices. The literary cycle reaches canonical form in the Ming novels Fengshen Yanyi and Xiyouji.
lore.originalScriptNote: The original script is 龍王 in traditional Chinese and 龙王 in simplified. The Pinyin reading Lóngwáng — two Tone-2 (rising) syllables — is the Modern Standard Mandarin citation form, recorded in the Unihan Database (kMandarin) and standard dictionaries. The tone-marked restoration keeps both acute accents as the display form; the registrable domain maps the accented vowels to their ASCII base letters, giving longwang. No syllable-boundary apostrophe is required: the segmentation lóng·wáng is unambiguous, so the display and domain forms differ only in the tone marks. Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct the Old Chinese forms as *[m]-roŋ (龍) and *[ɢ]ʷaŋ (王).
